# Summary

Permutation tests replace a theoretical reference distribution with one generated by rearrangements of the observed data. The rearrangements must be valid under the null hypothesis: unrestricted shuffling is inappropriate when observations are temporally or spatially ordered, clustered, blocked, or collected using a hierarchical experimental design. `permute` is an R package for describing such exchangeability structures and generating permutation indices from them. Its principal design vocabulary and restricted permutation designs were developed from those introduced by Cajo J. F. ter Braak in CANOCO 3.1 and refined in later CANOCO versions [@terBraak1990; @terBraakSmilauer2012]. `permute` makes these ideas available as reusable, model-independent R objects. Users can generate individual permutations, sets of permutations, or complete enumerations, while package authors can accept the same design objects in different statistical procedures. The package supports free permutations, cyclic shifts for series and transects, toroidal shifts for rectangular grids, blocks, plots, and nested or split-plot designs. 

# Statement of need

The validity of a permutation test rests on exchangeability under the null hypothesis [@lehmannRomano2005, sec. 15.2; @hemerikGoeman2018]. When all observations are exchangeable, a random ordering from `sample()` may suffice. Many real data sets have a more constrained structure. Repeated observations from a site cannot be exchanged freely with observations from other sites; the order of a time series or transect should be retained; a regular spatial grid may require shifts that preserve neighbourhood relationships; and whole plots and subplots may need to be permuted at different levels.

Encoding these restrictions separately in every analysis function is difficult to test and encourages subtle inconsistencies. `permute` separates the permutation design from both the data and the test statistic. A design constructed once can be inspected, checked, updated, enumerated, and passed to downstream software. This serves two audiences: analysts who need valid randomisations for non-trivial sampling designs, and package developers who need a stable interface for adding permutation inference to their own methods. With few required dependencies, `permute` gives other R packages a simple way to generate permutations for the models they already use.

# State of the field

CANOCO is a statistical software package for multivariate data analysis, ordination, and regression. Originally developed in the 1980s, it is widely used in ecology, environmental science, and related fields. CANOCO established a practical vocabulary for Monte Carlo permutation tests in ecological ordination, including unrestricted permutations, cyclic shifts for time series or linear transects, toroidal shifts for rectangular grids, blocks, and hierarchical or split-plot restrictions [@terBraak1990; @terBraak1992; @terBraakSmilauer2012]. The corresponding schemes in `permute` derive directly from this work. The cyclic and toroidal shift procedures relate to the spatial Monte Carlo testing literature discussed by @besagClifford1989.

R software involving permutations falls into several overlapping groups (@tbl-package-comparison). Test-oriented packages supply inferential procedures: for example, `coin` implements conditional inference for independence problems [@hothorn2008coin], `exactRankTests` provides exact rank and permutation tests [@exactRankTests], `flip` supplies multivariate permutation and rotation tests [@flip], `lmPerm` targets linear models [@lmPerm], and `permuco` covers regression, repeated-measures ANOVA/ANCOVA, and signal comparisons [@frossardRenaud2021]. Combinatorics packages instead generate or manipulate mathematical arrangements: for example, `arrangements`, `RcppAlgos`, and `gtools` enumerate permutations and combinations [@arrangements; @RcppAlgos; @gtools], while `partitions` and `permutations` address integer or set partitions and algebraic permutations respectively [@hankin2006; @hankinWest2007; @hankin2020]. `randomizeR` generates and evaluates treatment-allocation procedures for clinical trials [@uschner2018]. Domain-facing packages such as `vegan` perform analyses and consume permutation designs [@vegan].

| Category | Examples | Purpose | Restrictions and statistics |
|---|---|---|---|
| \rowcolor{permuteStripe} Statistical tests | `coin`, `permuco`, `flip` | Test-specific inference | Method-dependent restrictions; statistics supplied |
| Combinatorics | `arrangements`, `RcppAlgos` | Enumerate mathematical arrangements | No exchangeability design or statistic |
| \rowcolor{permuteStripe} Trial allocation | `randomizeR` | Generate treatment sequences | Allocation rules; assessments supplied |
| Analysis | `vegan` | Ecological analyses | Consumes `permute` designs; statistics supplied |
| \rowcolor{permuteStripe} Design infrastructure | `permute` | Generate admissible rearrangements | Series, grids, blocks, plots, and hierarchies; no statistic |

Table: Roles of selected R packages related to permutations. {#tbl-package-comparison tbl-colwidths="[23,16,28,33]"}

The distinct role of `permute` is therefore to represent admissible rearrangements independently of the statistic evaluated on them.

# Software design

In `permute`, a permutation design has three composable levels. @tbl-permutation-designs summarises the available schemes and restrictions.

::: {#tbl-permutation-designs .sideways-table}

```{=latex}
\begin{tabular}{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.18}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.27}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.31}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.24}}@{}}
\toprule
Concept & What changes & What is preserved or required & Control \\
\midrule
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Free permutation & Samples or whole plots are reordered freely within the group being permuted. & Membership of the group being permuted stays fixed. & \texttt{type = "free"} in \texttt{Within()} or \texttt{Plots()} \\
Cyclic shift & Samples or whole plots shift along a series or transect with wraparound. & Adjacency in the circular sequence is preserved. Optional reflection reverses the sequence. & \texttt{type = "series"} in \texttt{Within()} or \texttt{Plots()} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Toroidal shift & Samples or whole plots shift along both axes of a rectangular grid with wraparound. & Grid neighbourhoods are preserved under wraparound. Optional reflection can be limited to one axis per permutation. & \texttt{type = "grid"} in \texttt{Within()} or \texttt{Plots()} \\
Fixed-size group assignment & Individual samples are reassigned to labelled groups. & Each group retains its original sample count. & \texttt{Plots(type = "partition")} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Whole-plot predictor assignment & Plot-level predictors, such as treatment labels, are reassigned jointly among plots. & Predictors must be constant within each plot. Samples and responses stay fixed. Sample counts may differ among plots. & \texttt{Plots(type = "free", variables = \textasciitilde{} treatment)} \\
Blocking & Permutations are carried out separately within blocks. & Block membership stays fixed. & \texttt{how(blocks = \textasciitilde{} block\_id)} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Whole-plot rearrangement & Whole plots move with their samples. & Sample counts must match among plots within each block, or across all plots in an unblocked design. & \texttt{Plots()} with \texttt{"free"}, \texttt{"series"}, or \texttt{"grid"} \\
Split-plot permutation & Whole plots and the samples within them can be rearranged at their respective levels. & Samples stay with their original plot. When whole plots are rearranged, sample counts must match within each block, or across all plots in an unblocked design. & Combine \texttt{Plots()} and \texttt{Within()} in \texttt{how()} \\
\rowcolor{permuteStripe} Fixed ordering at one level & Permutations can proceed at the other level. & The chosen level retains its original ordering. & \texttt{type = "none"} in \texttt{Plots()} or \texttt{Within()} \\
Common within-plot permutation & The same rearrangement is applied within each plot in a block. & Plots must have equal sample counts. & \texttt{Within(constant = TRUE)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
```

Permutation design concepts in `permute` 0.10-1.

:::

Blocks are the outermost level: observations are never permute between blocks. Plots sit within blocks and may themselves be permuted. The within level controls rearrangement of observations inside plots and blocks, or of the whole data set when no higher levels are present. `how()` combines these components, while `Plots()` and `Within()` configure their behaviour. Block and plot strata may be supplied directly or described using formulas.

For example, the following design keeps sites within blocks and observations within sites, applies a common cyclic time shift to the sites in each block, and creates a reusable matrix of permutation indices:

```r
library("permute")

dat <- data.frame(
  block = gl(4, 12),
  site = gl(8, 6)
)
ctrl <- how(
  plots = Plots(strata = ~ site, type = "none"),
  within = Within(type = "series", constant = TRUE),
  blocks = ~ block,
  nperm = 999,
  data = dat
)
set.seed(42)
perms <- shuffleSet(nrow(dat), control = ctrl)
```

Additional support functions are provided by `permute`. For example, `check()` validates whether a requested design can be applied, `numPerms()` counts its possible permutations, and `allPerms()` enumerates sufficiently small sets. For permutations of observations, `shuffle()` returns a single permutation and `shuffleSet()` returns a matrix whose rows are permutation indices and which can be reused across statistics or parallel workers. `permutations()` applies generated permutation indices to a vector, while `permutator()` offers sequential access to a supplied or generated set. Stored design metadata and compatibility with R's seeded random-number generator support reproducible analyses.

# Worked example

The `CO2` data distributed with R contain carbon dioxide uptake curves for twelve plants of *Echinochloa crus-galli* from Quebec and Mississippi [@potvin1990]. Half of the plants from each source location were chilled overnight, and uptake was measured at seven ambient carbon dioxide concentrations. To test for an overall chilling effect, plants may be exchanged within source location, but each plant's seven-point response curve must remain intact. The design therefore treats source location (`Type`) as blocks, plants as plots, and observations within plants as fixed.

```{r}
#| label: co2-design
library("permute")

data("CO2", package = "datasets")
co2 <- as.data.frame(CO2)

ctrl <- how(
  blocks = ~ Type,
  plots = Plots(strata = ~ Plant, type = "free"),
  within = Within(type = "none"),
  nperm = 9999,
  data = co2
)
```

In this study, there are `{r} ctrl |> getBlocks() |> nlevels()` blocks and `{r} ctrl |> getPlots() |> getStrata() |> nlevels()` plots

```{r}
#| label: co2-design-blocks-plants
ctrl |> getBlocks() |> nlevels()
ctrl |> getPlots() |> getStrata() |> nlevels()
```

As the test statistic, we'll use the difference in mean uptake between chilled and non-chilled plants, averaged over the measured concentrations. `permutations()` applies the permutations directly to the response: the resulting `uptake` matrix has one row of shuffled uptake values per permutation.

```{r}
#| label: co2-test
effect <- function(y) {
  with(co2,
    mean(y[Treatment == "chilled"]) -
      mean(y[Treatment == "nonchilled"])
  )
}

set.seed(20261120)
uptake <- permutations(co2$uptake, control = ctrl)
observed <- effect(co2$uptake)
null <- apply(uptake, 1, effect)
p_value <- (sum(abs(null) >= abs(observed)) + 1) /
  (length(null) + 1)

# show observed difference of means and permutation p value
observed |> round(4)
p_value |> round(4)
```

The observed mean difference is $\approx$ `{r} observed |> round(2)` μ mol m^-2^ s^-1^, with a two-sided Monte Carlo p-value of `{r} p_value |> round(4)`. The simple test statistic keeps the example focused on the exchangeability design: unrestricted shuffling would incorrectly separate repeated measurements from the plants on which they were made.

# Research impact statement

`permute` originated as permutation infrastructure within the `vegan` package, and was later separated into its own package so that the same implementation could be used by other analysts and package authors. It has been developed publicly for more than fifteen years and has been distributed through CRAN since 2011. At the time of writing, 25 CRAN packages directly depend on or import `permute`, with a further four Bioconductor packages importing from `permute`. These include `vegan`, `permuco`, `randomizationInference`, `indicspecies`, and `codyn`, spanning community ecology, experimental analysis, randomisation inference, indicator-species analysis, and temporal diversity research. `permute` has been directly cited 415 times (Google Scholar; at the time of writing) and has been downloaded from CRAN at least 6.9 million times (although many of these will be due to downloads of `vegan`, which has a hard dependency on `permute`).

This use reflects the value of separating design generation from model fitting. `vegan`, for example, exposes `permute` controls across permutation-based ordination and ecological testing rather than maintaining a separate representation of blocks and restricted designs. Other packages can accept either a control object produced by `how()` or a pre-generated matrix of permutations, giving users a consistent way to state the randomisation design and making it easier to reproduce exactly the set of permutations used in an analysis. The result is focused permutation infrastructure: `permute` does not attempt to select a test statistic or fit an analysis model, but provides the exchangeability layer on which those procedures can rely.
